content.title: CA bill nicknamed 'Stop Nick Shirley Act' raises concerns about limiting journalism
content.text: WASHINGTON (TNND) — Iran’s reported seizure of two ships is raising new questions about whether Tehran will continue using the Strait of Hormuz as leverage, even as President Donald Trump says the U.S. ceasefire with Iran has been extended.Veteran Israeli diplomat Shahar Azani, a former spokesperson for Israel’s consulate general, said Iran is trying to “disrupt international commerce” and “exert pressure on the United States and its allies to end the war against Iran,” including through what he described as “continuous disruption.” (TNND)Veteran Israeli diplomat Shahar Azani, a former spokesperson for Israel’s consulate general, said Iran is trying to “disrupt international commerce” and “exert pressure on the United States and its allies to end the war against Iran,” including through what he described as “continuous disruption.”A social media post circulating online, described as coming from an Iranian negotiator, says a complete ceasefire “only makes sense if it is not violated by the maritime blockade.” Asked whether the Strait of Hormuz could remain a bargaining chip amid the ceasefire delay, Oseni said Iran is using “whatever it can,” but argued the U.S., Israel and Gulf states have shown “tenacity” in response.Azani also downplayed what the ship seizures indicate about Iran’s broader naval strength, saying disruptions could include “mere minds or even shooting at those ships,” and calling it “no indication of their overall naval capabilities.” He said, “Every terrorist organization is able to disrupt,” and described Iran’s position as reflecting “the level of degradation that they have reached as a result of the continuous American and Israeli campaign against this dictatorial regime.”The developments come as Israel’s attacks against Hezbollah continue and as Israel and Lebanon are expected to meet in Washington, D.C., this Thursday.Azani said he hopes any ceasefire holds, arguing Israel and Lebanon “have no bones to pick between them” and calling Hezbollah “the only disrupter for regional peace and stability,” describing it as “an Iranian proxy.” He said, “They want to keep Hezbollah intact. We want to disarm Hezbollah for the benefit of Israel and Lebanon.”Azani also pointed to Hezbollah’s history, saying, “Let’s remind our viewers, Hezbollah is the same organization that killed 241 Marines in 1983.” He called Hezbollah “an anti-Israel, anti-American, anti-West terrorist organization,” and said, “it needs to go away for peace and stability to come to the region.”Looking ahead to the Washington meetings on Thursday, Azani said the talks themselves are significant, saying, “The fact that we actually have the meetings is a tremendous achievement because under Lebanese law, Israelis and Lebanese cannot even engage in any kind of act of normalization.” He said he hopes the discussions help “empower the Lebanese people and the government” toward “dismantling” Hezbollah and “achieving a lasting peace between Israel and Lebanon, and sovereignty for the Lebanese people to gain back their own country.”
